title: A. Paññāvaddho: The mental aggregates, or nāma khandhas, of feeling, memory, thought and consciousness are also bound up with the surface motion. The fundamental ignorance,…
content:
How Fundamental Ignorance Infuses and Modifies the Citta

The mental aggregates, or nāma khandhas, of feeling, memory, thought and consciousness are also bound up with the surface motion. The fundamental ignorance, or avijjā, which permeates the ordinary citta and influences its knowing, uses the functions of these mental aggregates to perceive objects, such as seeing forms and hearing sounds. When the citta is modified in this way, we call it consciousness, being that function which acknowledges sensations. The citta is modified in that way because avijjā, which has been infused into the citta, usurps the citta and uses the citta’s power to its own ends.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: We all have habitual ways of doing things. We use habitual modes of thinking, behaving and understanding. So often these habits determine our…
content:
The Persistence of Habitual Modes of Thinking

We all have habitual ways of doing things. We use habitual modes of thinking, behaving and understanding. So often these habits determine our mental state, making it difficult to realize what the truth is; making it difficult to be present. Even when we are focused in the present, our habitual ways are hovering in the background. If our attention lapses a bit, they take over straightaway. The only way to overcome that tendency is to continue practicing the modes of training in Dhamma until the situation is seen more and more clearly. Then we begin to realize how delusory those concepts of past and future are; how they are not at all real.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "We can begin to discern this process only by carefully investigating how it operates in our own minds. As a first step, we…
content:
Investigating the Spontaneous Appearance of the "I"

"We can begin to discern this process only by carefully investigating how it operates in our own minds. As a first step, we should examine how this works in our everyday experiences. A thought arises, and instantly follows the notion 'I am thinking.' An emotion surfaces, and immediately appears 'I am angry' or 'I am happy.' A physical sensation occurs, and at once emerges 'I am in pain' or 'I feel good.' At each moment, the misunderstanding that these experiences have something solid behind them comes together with tanha—the craving to be a continuing entity—and out of the intersection of these elemental forces arises the strong conviction that 'this is me, this is mine, this is who I am.'"

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "With patience and perseverance, we allow our practice to gradually mature until the heart is ripe for enlightenment. It's quite interesting that compassion…
content:
Compassion Arising from Freedom from Suffering

"With patience and perseverance, we allow our practice to gradually mature until the heart is ripe for enlightenment. It's quite interesting that compassion isn't listed among the 10 paramis, but there's wisdom in this omission. True compassion—not the ordinary kind of pity we feel but the profound understanding of others' suffering—naturally arises only when we've gained enough freedom from our own suffering to be able to look back on those who are still hopelessly trapped in a world of pain and delusion. Because only someone who has found their way out of a dark and dangerous forest can truly understand the predicament of those still lost within it. When we practice diligently and correctly, the mental defilements start to loosen their grip, and we experience a profound shift in our understanding."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: All five senses work in much the same way, in that they are sensitive receptors that react to stimulation caused by contact with…
content:
The Mechanics of the Sensory Receptors

All five senses work in much the same way, in that they are sensitive receptors that react to stimulation caused by contact with external objects. That contact, in turn, sets up a train of electro-chemical pulses that travels through the sensory nerves, terminating in the brain. This, in brief, is the regular scientific view. So it is convenient for us to accept it as a suitable starting point. Let us analyze one sense faculty, sight, as typical of them all. Say an object, such as a tree, is seen. Light reflects off all the relevant parts of the tree, and a small part of this light enters our eyes. Due to the geometry of optics, this light displays a small image of the tree upside down on the retina, much as a camera acts in taking a photo.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "You should understand that hatred and anger are deeply interconnected, though they operate on different levels of time and awareness. Hatred tends to…
content:
How Hatred and Resentment Create a Self-Reinforcing Cycle of Suffering

"You should understand that hatred and anger are deeply interconnected, though they operate on different levels of time and awareness. Hatred tends to be a more sustained defilement that can act as both a source and an amplifier of anger. When hatred is an underlying condition in the mind, it lowers the threshold for anger to arise. Because pre-existing hatred has prepared the mind to react with anger, someone harboring hatred becomes angry more quickly and more intensely when encountering the objects of their aversion. Resentment adds yet another layer of suffering by refusing to let go of past wrongs. It holds on to grievances, keeping them fresh in our minds, not allowing wounds to heal or memories to fade. Resentment constantly rehearses the story of being wronged, ensuring that each new interaction is colored by past pain. This accumulated bitterness becomes readily available fuel for reigniting anger again and again. Working together, these defilements create what we might call a self-reinforcing cycle of suffering. Aversion prevents us from truly understanding others; ill will makes us quick to judge them harshly; hatred convinces us they are inherently flawed and cannot change; while resentment ensures we never forget our grievances. Each mental state feeds the others, making our anger feel increasingly vindicated."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: Most people believe that they are the body. If you believe that this body is actually you, then surely you should want to…
content:
Realizing the Body is Not the Self

Most people believe that they are the body. If you believe that this body is actually you, then surely you should want to know more about yourself. You have all this knowledge about the world and how it functions, so why do you leave out the one thing that is most important – yourself? Why not try to get to know yourself? And the first step is to question the physical body because it is the most gross part of oneself. If we contemplate the body in the proper way we eventually come to see clearly that this body is not oneself. It comes from this world, it returns to this world, it is part of this world. It is all made of atomic structure – atoms, molecules and chemicals – and it does not exist apart from these things.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Ajaan Mahā Boowa said when he first became a bhikkhu, he studied all the Pāli texts. He achieved the level of mahā in…
content:
The Relationship Between Scriptural Study and Actual Practice

"Ajaan Mahā Boowa said when he first became a bhikkhu, he studied all the Pāli texts. He achieved the level of mahā in Pāli. He read the Ti-pitaka in Pāli. When he went to Ajaan Mun, Ajaan Mun told him that he mustn’t bother about what he’d learnt from the books, saying that it would be of no use to him for a long time. Later on, he would find what he had learnt to be quite valuable, but not yet. In other words, he had to practice the Dhamma first. Then he could refer back to the books and immediately understand their meaning. What he had learnt, he could then see in his own practice. The saññā and the paññā would blend together. That’s very valuable. That’s partly why Ajaan Mahā Boowa can give such good talks now. If he could only talk from the books, his talks wouldn’t inspire in the same way."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "When we die, the latent desire for bodily existence leads us to grasp another body; that is how the round of rebirth continues.…
content:
Severing Attachment and Understanding the Essence of Mind (Citta)

"When we die, the latent desire for bodily existence leads us to grasp another body; that is how the round of rebirth continues. The only way to break this circuit is to sever the attachment that causes it. In the beginning, we investigate the body to find out that this body is not me. It is made of earthly substance and, in the end, it goes back to the earth. By seeing that truth, we lose the fear of death, realizing: 'This isn’t me. I don’t die. I go on, but the body doesn’t'. The body dies, but that which is left we call the 'citta'—the essence of mind that knows. Knowingness does not depend on material substance. The citta is really important because within it are the defilements as well as the Dhamma, the right way, the truth."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "In addition, the practice of morality will bring you a certain degree of contentment in everyday life. It brings the satisfaction of knowing…
content:
Contentment and the Subtle Discontent of the Mind

"In addition, the practice of morality will bring you a certain degree of contentment in everyday life. It brings the satisfaction of knowing that you have done nothing wrong, and that no one can rightly claim that you have behaved wrongly. That knowledge brings with it a measure of freedom and a comforting feeling that you are unblemished where the world is concerned. At the same time, you will experience a certain mental restlessness due to wanting, craving, and hankering for objects of attachment. In other words, dissatisfaction is there, but it is experienced in a more subtle manner than the discontent suffered from lack of morality. To overcome that level of discontent you must turn your attention to training the mind."
